claims.text: Conventionally sintering high-purity ZrB2 above 2300 °C produces a single-phase ceramic.
Conventionally sintered single-phase ZrB2 is porous.
SPS can consolidate single-phase ZrB2 below 2300 °C.
An SPS temperature range of approximately 1900–2100 °C is suitable for consolidating ZrB2.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will be denser and less porous than conventionally sintered ZrB2.
SPS-processed ZrB2 will resist liquid-plating-bath-induced degradation better than conventionally sintered ZrB2.
Rapid pulsed heating and uniaxial pressure during SPS enhance ZrB2 densification.
Rapid heating and applied pressure accelerate diffusion and particle rearrangement in ZrB2.
Accelerated diffusion and particle rearrangement enable effective ZrB2 densification at lower temperatures.
SPS limits excess grain growth in ZrB2.
SPS minimizes pore formation and produces a refined ZrB2 microstructure with improved grain connectivity.
Pores and microstructural flaws in conventionally sintered ZrB2 act as sites for liquid ingress.
Liquid ingress through pores and flaws promotes degradation during long-term plating-bath service.
Reduced porosity from SPS will enhance the mechanical strength of ZrB2.
Reduced porosity and enhanced strength will delay or reduce hole formation and structural failure during extended plating-bath exposure.
Conventionally prepared ZrB2 typically has greater porosity and more microstructural flaws than the proposed SPS material.
A service exposure duration of approximately 500–1000 hours is relevant for evaluating performance in a liquid plating environment.
The proposed comparison uses conventionally sintered ZrB2 as a control against ZrB2 processed by SPS at 1900–2100 °C.
